title: Test the spirits (1 John 4:1–6)
hook: not every voice is from God; test it

segments.voice: Yesterday, the heart that condemns, and your line was greater than your heart. When the inner prosecutor started up, did you say the line? Day six hundred eighty-eight.

Before there were labs, people tested gold by rubbing it on a dark stone and looking at the streak it left. Real gold left one color. Fakes left another. The stone was called a touchstone, and its lesson was simple: something can look exactly like gold and not be gold. Yesterday First John spoke gently to the heart that condemns itself. Now the writer turns brisk and practical: don't believe every voice. Test it.

In the King James Bible: "Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God: because many false prophets are gone out into the world." Try, here, translates a Greek word that was also used for testing metal, an assayer's word. Notice he starts with beloved. This isn't a cynic talking. It's someone who loves his readers enough to want them not to be fooled. In his day, it seems, teachers were going around claiming the Spirit, and some of them said that Jesus didn't really come in a body. So the writer gives a test that fits his moment: "Every spirit that confesseth that Jesus Christ is come in the flesh is of God." Remember the opening of the letter: what our hands have handled. The test is whether a teaching holds on to a real, touchable Jesus. Then a word of courage: "greater is he that is in you, than he that is in the world." The reader isn't small and helpless before every persuasive voice. And then a sobering line: the world listens to its own. Popular doesn't mean true. Christians call this gift discernment. Paul lists the discerning of spirits among the Spirit's gifts. Over the centuries, churches have taught many ways to practice it. Catholic and Orthodox teaching weighs a claim against Scripture read with the church's tradition. Protestant teaching holds Scripture as the final test, often weighed with the counsel of a community. Ignatius of Loyola wrote rules for discerning the spirits that are still taught today. Each starts where the writer does: some voices sound like gold, and the letter says to test them before trusting them.
screen: `GREATER IS HE THAT IS IN YOU.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: check one claim before believing it. Settle, and breathe. Think of something you heard or read this week that you accepted quickly. A headline, a rumor, a confident voice online, an inner voice that told you something about yourself. Hold it up like gold on a touchstone. Where did it come from? Who benefits if I believe it? Does it lead toward love, or away from it? Does it fit what I know to be true? Don't rush to a verdict. Just test it. If you pray, you can ask for discernment. The bell holds the time.
Discernment. The gift of testing voices before trusting them, the way a touchstone tells real gold from fake.
Your line: like gold on a touchstone. Today, before you share or repeat one thing, check where it came from. Day six hundred eighty-eight.

howItsDone: Christians practice discernment by testing teachings against Scripture and the faith of the church, and some seek the help of a pastor, spiritual director or community; Ignatian discernment, from Ignatius of Loyola, is still taught today.

original.note: Greek: to test, assay, prove, as with metals. the word behind 'try the spirits'.

trapdoor: what you thought: be suspicious of everyone.
what it means: love includes testing voices, and the letter's test is a real, fleshly Jesus.
what a scholar hears: dokimazō, a verb also used for assaying metal, aimed at teachers who seem to have denied Jesus came in the flesh, and a gift Paul calls discerning of spirits.

notes: Touchstone history (streak test on dark stone): standard. The claim that this use 'gave us the word' was cut in review.
The opponents' teaching (Jesus not truly in the flesh) is a scholarly reconstruction; hedged with 'it seems'.
Summaries of Catholic/Orthodox and Protestant approaches to discernment: confirm fairness.
The practice extends 'test the spirits' to everyday claims; the script keeps the letter's own test distinct.

Editor review (2026-10-01): cut the touchstone etymology and the 'Jewelers still test metals' aside; replaced 'First John has been all warmth... without warning' (2:18–27 already warned of antichrists) with a callback to day 687; softened dokimazō from 'the word for testing metal' to 'also used for testing metal' (teach, match, myth, trapdoor); restated the Catholic/Orthodox and Protestant approaches as church teaching rather than 'often/many' claims; softened 'many still use' and 'widely used'.
